structure.title: 5. Properties of the basic CU model (incl. calibration and impulse responses)

observations.statement: The firm-level empirical framework writes relative demand as a function of relative capacity and relative price plus an attractiveness residual; the parameter of interest is the capacity elasticity of demand and the null hypothesis is that it is zero (no capacity competition). It is rewritten in quarterly differences so that sector aggregates are absorbed by a sector-by-time fixed effect.

The endogeneity threat is spelled out: anticipated changes in a firm's attractiveness could raise both capacity and realized demand. The remedy is to condition on the lagged information set the firm used to forecast, relying on the assumption that capacity changes observed now were decided on information at least one quarter old (gestation lag).

Because current price changes may still correlate with the unpredictable attractiveness innovation, the expected price change surveyed a quarter earlier instruments the realized price change. Exclusion is argued from timing: an expectation formed before the quarter cannot be correlated with an innovation that occurred within the quarter.

The one-quarter timing assumption for capacity is justified in footnotes by citing the time-to-build literature on gestation periods, by noting it is the standard lag in business cycle models and in the paper's own model, and by pointing to a supplementary appendix robustness analysis.

The reduced-form demand equation used in the empirical section is asserted in footnotes to be the same as the demand function later derived from the model, and the derived elasticities are discussed as special cases of a more general specification with imperfect substitutes.

Sources for the stylized facts are named in text and table notes: the Federal Reserve Board and BEA for the U.S., the DG ECFIN Business and Consumer Survey and OECD for the euro area, the KOF business tendency survey for Switzerland, and plant-level results cited from prior work on the Census QPC. Table notes give start dates by series and a common end date.

The firm-level KOF survey microdata are restricted and were obtained through the KOF micro data centre; the dataset description is delegated to Supplementary Appendix A and to a cited earlier paper that uses the same data.

The number of observations is reported in every column of the three firm-level regression tables; the IV samples are much smaller than the OLS samples because the identification design requires lagged expectation variables that are available for fewer firm-quarters.

The regression unit is the firm-quarter in Swiss manufacturing, with firms indexed within sectors; the stylized-fact correlations use sector-level quarterly series. The survey is described as quarterly for capacity utilization and monthly for demand changes.

The Bayesian estimation matches four detrended U.S. macro series (real consumption, real investment, real exogenous expenditure, hours); the description of the series and their construction is placed in a supplementary appendix rather than the main text.

The firm-level long-term underutilization table presents rows under successively stricter sampling criteria (all firms, then firms with a minimum number of years observed) so that the reader can see how the pattern changes with panel length.

Survey responses on demand, price, capacity, expectations and assessments are qualitative three-valued codes (decrease, unchanged, increase, or too large, adequate, too small) and are entered directly as regressors and outcomes in linear regressions.

Because quarterly demand changes were only surveyed in recent years, a quarterly demand change is also implied from monthly responses using a sign-consistency rule with missing assigned otherwise; an alternative averaging rule is used in a supplementary appendix and reported as giving similar results.

The surveyed expected demand change is explicitly treated as an imperfect measure of the firm's expectation: it is interpreted as one piece of information in the conditioning set rather than a sufficient statistic that would absorb the effect of predetermined capacity.

The information-set controls are enumerated by group in the main text (expected changes, historical changes, and level assessments of several business variables) with the full list deferred to a supplementary appendix; firm size (employees), age and age squared are also included per the table notes.

Cyclical correlations and business cycle moments are computed on HP-filtered logged series with the standard quarterly smoothing parameter, stated in table notes; the Solow residual is constructed under an assumed Cobb-Douglas production function with a fixed labour share, stated once in a footnote as applying throughout.

observations.statement: The IV table pairs a baseline column with a column adding an interaction, for each of two outcome measures; each column reports the first-stage F-statistic and N. The notes state that the information set, size, age, age squared, firm fixed effects and sector-by-time fixed effects are controlled for and that standard errors are clustered by firm.

A bivariate OLS table with default standard errors is shown first as a correlation benchmark, followed by the identified IV table with controls, fixed effects and clustered errors; the text explicitly contrasts the two as correlation versus identification.

The limiting-factor table regresses binary indicators on the capacity utilization rate with firm and sector-by-time fixed effects and size-age controls, listing FE and controls as Yes rows and reporting an F-statistic and N per column; no R-squared or dependent-variable mean is shown in any regression table.

Calibrated parameters are reported in a three-column table (parameter, value, target matched) with the data source and period for each target described in the surrounding text; the estimated model uses a larger set of targets that are held fixed during estimation.

Standard errors are clustered at the firm level in the fixed-effects and IV tables and left as default OLS errors in the bivariate table; the choice of cluster level is stated only in table notes and no justification or cluster count is given in the text.
observations.locator: Table 4 notes, Table 5 notes, Table 6 notes

observations.statement: Uncertainty for the cyclical correlation coefficients in the descriptive tables is reported as estimated standard deviations computed with the VARHAC method, cited to its originators in the table notes and in a footnote.

For the structural model, parameters not pinned down by calibration targets are given posterior distributions via Bayesian estimation; the variance decomposition is computed at posterior modes, and priors, posteriors and estimation details are placed in supplementary appendices.
A first-stage F-statistic is reported as a row in every IV column of the main table; no separate first-stage table is shown and the text does not comment on instrument strength.

Model fit is diagnosed by backing out structural shocks with the Kalman smoother, feeding a single shock type into the estimated models, and tabulating standard deviations and covariances with output of the fitted series next to the same statistics from U.S. data.

Robustness of the firm-level evidence to the lag assumption and to an alternative construction of the quarterly demand measure is delegated to supplementary appendix sections and mentioned only in footnotes, each with a one-sentence summary that results are robust.

The model's properties are established by side-by-side comparison with benchmark models: impulse responses of the basic model versus Leontief-RBC and Cobb-Douglas-RBC versions, and variance decompositions and moments of the estimated full model versus a full variable-utilization model estimated with a procedure kept as close as possible; benchmark details are in appendices.

A single heterogeneity check interacts the capacity change with the firm's lagged assessment of its capacity level to see whether the demand response differs when firms view capacity as too large or too small; it is introduced as interesting to see and reported in the main IV table.
observations.locator: Section 3.3 last paragraph, Table 6 columns 2 and 4

observations.statement: Since all variables are qualitative codes, coefficient magnitudes are interpreted as changes in the probabilities of reporting a demand decrease or increase, decomposed in text and a footnote and reconciled with the OLS coefficient; IV coefficients are described as somewhat smaller but substantial.

Impulse responses are read in log deviations from steady state for a one percentage point shock, and the size of the investment response is explained with a back-of-envelope link through the depreciation rate.

The forecast error variance decomposition at a ten-year horizon is the headline quantitative result and is related in the introduction to recent empirical papers that attribute business cycles to a single demand-type shock, and contrasted with prior models needing multiple shocks.
The author flags that the firm-level dataset covers only manufacturing, notes that casual observation suggests the mechanism in services, and labels service-sector evidence as future research.

A possible objection (low real wage volatility under a single shock) is anticipated in a footnote, answered by arguing that low volatility is what a model should predict for an acyclical series, and backed by a supplementary appendix result with all shocks present.

The downward trend in the aggregate utilization series is acknowledged in the first footnote; the author states the paper does not explain the trend and deliberately shows the unprocessed series, deferring discussion to a supplementary appendix.

A drawback of the basic model (lack of persistence in the investment response) is acknowledged in a footnote and addressed by adding adjustment costs in the extended model; compatible extensions with other mechanisms are listed.

The mechanism (capacity competition) is tested with firm-level survey regressions whose specification is derived from the model's demand function; the evidence is framed as showing the mechanism is empirically plausible rather than as a structural estimate.

Survey questions about the main factor limiting production are used to discriminate between demand-driven and cost-driven explanations of underutilization, and to argue in footnotes that competing models contradict the survey pattern.

Regression tables use three-level significance stars with thresholds defined in the notes; notes also state the standard error type, variable definitions, the controls and fixed effects, and the data source with its sample period.

The paper has two figures: a raw aggregate time series with NBER recessions shaded and the source stated in the caption, and a grid of impulse responses overlaying three models with distinct line styles for transitory and persistent shocks.

Descriptive fact tables list region and sector rows with start dates, averages, standard deviations, shares of periods below thresholds and cyclical correlations with their estimated standard deviations in parentheses; abbreviations are expanded in the notes.

Supplementary appendices are lettered (A through K) and referenced throughout for data description, model extensions, proofs, benchmark calibrations, estimation details and further discussion; they are hosted online and are not part of the text read here.
observations.locator: footnotes and section cross-references; Supplementary Data statement

observations.statement: The introduction previews the firm-level finding, the estimated variance shares and the benchmark comparisons, then closes with an explicit three-item contribution paragraph and a section-by-section roadmap.

The empirical material comes before the model: motivating stylized facts, then the identified firm-level evidence with its own framework and identification subsections, then the basic model, its properties and calibration, then estimation; there is no separate robustness section.

Related-literature positioning is woven into the introduction and its footnotes with model-by-model contrasts rather than a separate literature section; long footnotes carry definitions, caveats and citations.

Theoretical results are stated as numbered definitions and a proposition in the main text with the proof deferred to a supplementary appendix; log-linearized conditions are displayed to explain dynamics before any numerical results.
A data availability statement says the KOF microdata cannot be shared publicly but that instructions for obtaining them, all other data and all code are deposited on Zenodo with a DOI.
The estimation platform (Dynare) and the solution method (log-linearization around the steady state) are named in a footnote; no software is named for the firm-level regressions.

Firm-level data come from a research institute's business tendency survey accessed through its micro data centre (credited in acknowledgments); the aggregate series are public statistics from central bank, statistical agency, European Commission and OECD sources.
observations.locator: Table notes, footnote 11, Acknowledgments, Data Availability Statement

observations.statement: Generalization beyond manufacturing is addressed by showing euro-area service-sector facts in the descriptive tables while conceding the identified firm-level evidence is manufacturing only.

To reduce the estimation burden, a set of steady-state targets is imposed throughout Bayesian estimation, so that the same number of parameters are pinned down as functions of the remaining estimated parameters; the targets and their data sources are described in text.

Each exogenous disturbance's stochastic process is written out (AR(1) for most, AR(2) for investment demand, with a cross-loading of investment shocks on consumption demand) and each modelling choice is motivated by a data pattern it is meant to capture.

Quantitative exposition isolates one shock at a time: numerical experiments with a transitory and a persistent demand disturbance in the calibrated model, and estimated-shock counterfactuals with all other shocks shut down in the estimated model.

gaps: No justification is given for clustering standard errors at the firm level, and the number of clusters is not reported.
No R-squared or mean of the dependent variable is reported in any regression table.
No summary statistics table for the regression variables (the descriptive tables cover aggregate facts only).
No balance, placebo or pre-trend style diagnostics for the firm-level design; the only design diagnostic is the first-stage F-statistic.
The sample period and construction of the macro series used in estimation are not stated in the main text (deferred to Supplementary Appendix I).
No preregistration, IRB or ethics statement (not expected for this design).
No software is named for the firm-level regressions; only Dynare is named for the structural estimation.
Supplementary appendices A-K are not part of the extracted text and were not read.

reading.note: All 35 pages of the extracted text were read in four chunks: main text pages 1-33 in full including footnotes and table notes; pages 33-35 (acknowledgments, data availability statement, reference list) read but the reference list was only skimmed. The supplementary appendices are online only and not included in the text file.
